## From Translation Yield to Observational Cosmology

A translation-yield engine becomes a cosmological theory when observations can distinguish its possible histories, sector realizations, and matter completions. The engine fixes where expansion enters. The sky must decide whether the construction built above it is viable.

### Redshift drift distinguishes yield histories

The endpoint mapping

$$
1+z=\frac{\chi_e}{\chi_o}
$$

constrains the yield values at two events, but different histories can share the same endpoint ratio. Redshift drift tests how that ratio changes while a source remains under observation. Its prediction must be derived by evolving the emission event, observation event, and intervening propagation kernel together. Importing the standard FLRW drift formula without that derivation would assume the correspondence that the test is meant to examine.

Redshift drift is therefore a particularly clean discriminator among candidate $\chi(t)$ histories.

Transient signals provide a second linked test. Once intrinsic source evolution and known propagation effects are controlled, wavelength stretching and duration stretching must share the same factor:

$$
\frac{\lambda_o}{\lambda_e}
=
\frac{\Delta t_o}{\Delta t_e}
=
1+z.
$$

A completion that reproduces spectral redshift but not the corresponding duration stretching would fail one of the engine's central signal predictions.

### Distance and brightness test geometry and transport

A candidate history must be turned into observable distances. Radial propagation interval, angular-diameter distance, luminosity distance, and lookback interval are not interchangeable. Their relations depend on the geometry, observer standards, and transport rules of the completed model.

Brightness sharpens the test. Observed flux depends on signal arrival rate, emitting area, angular spreading, photon counting, source evolution, and any lensing or attenuation along the path. The duration relation supplies an arrival-interval factor, but a luminosity-distance law must show how all factors combine. Tolman-style surface-brightness behavior and distance reciprocity then test whether the proposed geometry and transport form one coherent system.

### Local metrology tests UYC realization

Universal Yield Covariance is exposed wherever two local standards could respond differently. Atomic, optical, hyperfine, molecular, nuclear, mechanical, and orbital clocks must remain mutually consistent to the required precision. Spectral ratios, recoil measurements, radar ranging, ephemerides, weak-equivalence tests, and bounds on dimensionless constants constrain the electromagnetic, gravitational, strong, and weak realization of the shared covariance principle.

Local consistency is not protected by the word “screening.” It is earned only if the relevant interactions and standards satisfy the UYC targets without forbidden dimensionless residuals.

### Thermal observations test cosmological consistency

The cosmic microwave background distinguishes a redshift dictionary from a thermodynamically complete cosmology. A viable model must account for blackbody integrity, the temperature–redshift relation, recombination, the visibility function, the acoustic scale, peak structure, damping, and the observed perturbation correlations.

Nucleosynthesis and baryon–photon bookkeeping test the same completion at earlier epochs. None of these results follows by treating cosmological redshift as photon momentum cooling; that would contradict the conservation placement of the present engine.

### Growth and lensing test matter dynamics

Universal signal yield does not by itself specify the motion and growth of massive structure. A completed model must derive the matter equations governing peculiar motion, collapse, clustering, lensing, and environmental response. Those equations may contain additional matter-sector structure, but that structure should not be hidden by reusing $\chi$ as an unexplained mobility factor.

Growth-rate measurements, redshift-space distortions, kinetic Sunyaev–Zel'dovich observations, lensing–clustering comparisons, baryon acoustic structure, and environment-dependent tests can then distinguish viable matter dynamics from a signal engine that never closes dynamically.

### A discriminating program

A serious translation-yield cosmology must face these tests together. Redshift drift selects among histories; linked spectral and duration stretching tests the signal package; distance and brightness test geometry and transport; local metrology tests UYC sector covariance; CMB and nucleosynthesis test thermal consistency; growth and lensing test matter dynamics. Success in one layer cannot compensate for contradiction in another.

This is the route from the Tier 2 physical engine to a Tier 3 theory that can be quantitatively compared with the sky.
